title: Kolkata Goes Beyond Idli-Dosa With Malabari Biryani, Chettinad Chicken and Banana-Leaf Feasts
excerpt: Two major hotel food festivals in the city spotlight lesser-known dishes from Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, serving everything from kaima-rice biryani to banana flower fritters.
body:
• Two major Kolkata hotels — Novotel and Fairfield by Marriott — hosted South Indian food festivals in late August, featuring regional cuisines from Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.
  • The menus go far beyond the standard idli-dosa-sambar, showcasing Thalassery Chicken Biryani, Madurai Mutton Chukka, Malabar Chemmeen Ularthiyathu and Kerala-style appam.
  • Chef Arun Vijayan at Fairfield by Marriott emphasizes keeping traditional recipes intact, noting that Kerala cuisine uses milder spices than Karnataka or Tamil Nadu.
  • The pop-ups reflect growing demand in Kolkata for authentic regional South Indian food served on banana leaves with traditional accompaniments.

Kolkata's food scene is venturing well past idli, dosa and sambar. Two of the city's major hotels ran dedicated South Indian food festivals in the last week of August, drawing diners with menus that spotlight the lesser-known dishes of Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka — from Malabari biryani cooked with kaima rice to Chettinad chicken and banana-leaf-served payasam.

Novotel's Culinary Safari

Novotel Kolkata Hotel & Residences in Newtown ran "Flavours of India — A Journey Through South India" from August 26 to 31 at its Ministry of Kebabs restaurant. Curated by Chef Anthony Da Salva, the festival brought together recipes from four southern states. The vegetarian menu featured Mangalore Paneer Ghee Roast, Mirapakaya Bajji and Vazhai Poo Vada — banana flower fritters that are a staple across Tamil Nadu and Kerala, according to The Travel and Tourism Times.

The non-vegetarian highlights included Madurai Mutton Chukka, Andhra Kodi Vepudu (a dry chicken preparation with bold chilli-based seasoning) and Malabar Chemmeen Ularthiyathu, a Kerala-style prawn stir-fry cooked with coconut. The festival also served Gongura Maamsam Koora, a lamb curry made with the tart sorrel leaves that are a signature of Andhra cuisine, alongside Chicken Chettinad and Thalassery Chicken Biryani.

Kerala on a Banana Leaf at Fairfield by Marriott

Across the city, Fairfield by Marriott hosted a separate Kerala-cuisine pop-up through August 30, led by Chef Arun Vijayan. The experience was designed as a traditional Kerala sadya-style meal, with food served on banana leaves and earthen bowls of warm water offered for hand-washing — a gesture that signals authenticity beyond the menu itself, according to Indulge Express.

"In Kolkata, people are expecting local and traditional food. We are not doing a fusion menu — we are keeping the traditional recipe intact and following it."

— Chef Arun Vijayan, Fairfield by Marriott Kolkata

The recommended dishes included Pineapple Fish Moilee, Chutta Kozhi Chaps, Meen Manga Curry, Kerala Chicken Roast and Kallappam — a soft, spongy rice pancake fermented with toddy that differs from the more widely known appam. Chef Vijayan noted that Kerala cuisine stands apart from its southern neighbors in spice intensity. "In Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, they use strong spices. But in Kerala, we use mild spices only," he told Indulge Express.

The Secret to Malabari Biryani

The Kerala-style biryani emerged as a highlight at both events. Unlike the more familiar Hyderabadi or Lucknowi biryanis built on long-grain basmati and heavy spice profiles, Malabari biryani uses kaima rice — a shorter, plumper grain that absorbs flavors differently. "Our biryani masala is not strong, and that gives more taste and flavour to the dish. The secret to a good Malabari biryani is the combination of kaima rice and meat," Chef Vijayan explained.

At Novotel, the Thalassery Chicken Biryani — named for the Malabar port town of Thalassery, where it originated — offered a similar take, with the restrained spicing that distinguishes Kerala's culinary approach from the bolder flavors of Andhra and Chettinad traditions.

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

For Indian communities abroad, the expansion of South Indian cuisine beyond the ubiquitous idli-dosa-sambar trio reflects a trend already visible in diaspora cities. Restaurants in the Bay Area, London and Toronto have been broadening their South Indian menus for years, but the fact that Kolkata — a city known for its own robust food culture — is embracing this diversity signals a deeper shift in how regional Indian cuisines are understood and consumed nationally.

Both festivals priced their menus in the Rs 1,649-1,899 range per person, positioning the experience as fine dining rather than casual street food — an acknowledgment that South Indian cuisine, in all its regional variety, belongs at the same table as any haute cuisine tradition.
